facts.text: Saffire-2 flew on CRS OA-5 (Cygnus) and burned nine smaller samples, each 29 cm x 5 cm.
Samples 5 and 6 were SIBAL fabric; one sample was a flat PMMA slab (identified as Sample 9 on p.181).
Two cameras recorded the burns at 30 frames per second, each imaging just over half of the sample.
The sample was illuminated with a green LED for 0.4 s every 2 s so the pyrolysis char front could be seen.
Pyrolysis front and base were tracked along the sample centerline; pyrolysis length is the distance between them.
In forced concurrent flow (20-25 cm/s) flames reached a quasi-steady state with limiting pyrolysis lengths of about 4-5 cm and spread rates around 2 mm/s.
The thick PMMA sample asymptotically reached a limiting length in microgravity.
Flame position curves show that SIBAL spread rate is steady for most of the Saffire-1 and Saffire-2 tests.
Flammability of silicone in microgravity appears to be reduced compared to normal gravity, at least for the flow speeds tested.
Nomex, a common material used on the ISS and rated 'safe', could not be ignited even when bathed by a pilot flame.
Under a variety of conditions, concurrent flames spreading over thin fuels achieved a limiting size in Saffire I-V, unlike normal-gravity upward spread.
Both concurrent thick PMMA samples in Saffire IV/V (IV-2, V-3) did not spread appreciably and advanced through surface regression only.
Extinguishment of bubbling polymers cannot be assumed to occur rapidly in quiescent conditions.
On the ISS, for fires detected by smoke detectors, software response automatically terminates intra- and inter-module ventilation for the affected module.
The ISS has a portable CO2 extinguisher for use in the U.S. modules and two types of water-based extinguishers for the Russian modules.
